scope.outOfScope.third-party-exporters.r.value: "out of scope permanently; bridge with a recording rule if an SLO needs them"

scope.outOfScope.paperclip-agent-health-.value: "Out of scope by category, not by grandfathering. It exports agent-fleet health gauges, not a request path; it has no requests to count. paperclip_* stays."

scope.outOfScope.instrumentation-and-slo.value: "Implementing this in any service, and the error-budget release gate, are not governed here. This is the contract the gate later rests on."

metrics.platform_request_duration_second.value: "Duration of one served request or one handled bus message, in seconds."

"From the moment the server has the request line and headers, to the moment the last byte of the response body is written or the connection fails. Middleware the service owns is inside the measurement; time the request spent queued in the kernel or the gateway is not."

"An SSE, websocket, long-poll or watch response (see streamClassification). The clock stops at establishment -- when the stream is established or the establishment fails -- NOT when the connection closes. Establishment is the moment the service starts waiting on something it does not control: the response headers written for SSE and other streamed bodies, the 101 written for a websocket upgrade, and for a long-poll or watch the moment the hold begins, whether or not headers have been flushed. A long-poll server holds its headers until data arrives, so \"headers written\" alone would measure the hold. A long-poll answered without holding, because data was already pending, is established when it responds. Closing a stream never records a second observation. `outcome` reports whether establishment succeeded. A service MUST NOT record a long-lived response's open lifetime into this family: one such observation lands in +Inf and permanently breaches any latency objective for the service, and it drags the p99 of every `sum by (service)` panel with it."

"A stream that establishes cleanly and then fails mid-flight is NOT captured here. That is a stated hole in v1, not an oversight: a terminal outcome recorded at close would be a second observation per attempt, which breaks cardinalRule and the one-denominator property the single instrument exists for. Stream lifetime and mid-flight failure get their own family under their own name (platform_stream_duration_seconds), which is additive and needs no v2 of this file. Until that lands, an SLO over kind=stream measures establishment only and must say so."

"What ends the response decides its kind, not how it is framed. A response that ends when the service finishes its own work is kind=http even when it is sent chunked or flushed incrementally: a large export is latency the caller waits for, and the latency SLI is right to count it. A response that ends when the client disconnects, a subscribed event arrives or a hold timeout expires is kind=stream. Waiting on a reply to work this request itself started (an HTTP-to-NATS request/reply bridge, a job it enqueued and awaits) is service-ended and kind=http: that wait is the caller's latency, not a hold. `kind` is fixed per route, so a route that can stream is declared kind=stream, or its streaming form is a separate route."

"From the moment the message is delivered to the handler, to the moment the handler acks, naks or terminates it. Time spent waiting for a redelivery is NOT included -- a redelivery is a separate delivery and a separate observation."
"From delivery of the request message to the publish of the reply, or to the moment the service abandons the request."

"Kubelet liveness, readiness and startup probes, and scrapes of the exposition path itself, are NOT observed into this family. They are not user traffic and they are not the service's promise to anybody. At an ordinary 10s probe period a homelab service runs roughly ten probes per user request, which divides the measured error ratio by about eleven: a user path failing 10% of the time reads 0.91% and pages nobody. It also puts a floor under the objective -- the probes are ten of every eleven observations and never fail, so the highest error ratio the family can express is 1/11 = 9.09% and a service cannot measure below about 90.9% availability however completely the user path fails, so \"99.5%\" stops being a statement about the user."

"Exclusion at the source, not a reserved route value the consumer must remember to filter out. A route value that every expression has to exclude is the `pod` and `instance` mistake again: correct in the example, dropped in the copy."

"The service's own health, readiness and liveness endpoints and exposition.path. A health endpoint that is also a real API surface for callers is a different endpoint and is observed; the test is who calls it, not what it is named."

metrics.platform_build_info.help.value: "Always 1. Carries the build identity that must never be a label on the RED family."

buckets.rationale.value: "Prometheus client defaults (5ms..10s) extended by one decade to 30s, because a control-plane request that takes 12s is a distinct failure mode from one that takes 40s and both are inside a 30s client timeout budget."

buckets.fifteenSecondBoundary.value: "Added because the NATS ack deadline sits at 30s, so every kind=pubsub handler in trouble that does not extend its deadline lands in the 10-to-30 bucket (an extending handler can reach +Inf; see errorClassification.bus.extendedHandlers). Across that gap a handler whose true p99 is 11s reports 20s; with this boundary it reports 12.5s. A 9-second error bar is not something to put in a page annotation, and without the boundary no latency threshold anywhere in the 10-30s band is expressible."

buckets.nativeHistograms.value: "Out of scope for v1. Argo Rollouts analysis and the deployed Prometheus must both work today, and classic buckets are the dull mechanism that does. A native histogram path is additive later: a new metric name, not a change to this one."

labels.required.service.rule.value: "The component's stable identifier -- the same identifier the component uses as the final segment of the component path in the CloudEvents `source` attribute (contracts/events/envelope.v1.schema.json). That segment's envelope pattern is wider (it admits dots and has no length limit), so a component picks a name valid under THIS pattern and uses it in both places. One name for a service on the bus and in the metrics, or correlating an event storm with a latency spike becomes a lookup table somebody maintains by hand."

labels.required.environment.rule.value: "Operator-supplied from the ConfigSet. No repository default and no enumerated value list: a fork names its own environments (ADR-029). It is set on the series by the service, NOT by Prometheus `externalLabels` -- external labels are applied on remote-write, federation and alert delivery, not on local queries, so a canary AnalysisTemplate querying the in-cluster Prometheus would never see them. Attaching it by ServiceMonitor relabeling was the other option and puts contract conformance into per-service GitOps YAML, which is the file most likely to differ in a fork."

labels.required.tenant.source.value: "PLATFORM_TENANT, or the per-request tenancy of the authenticated principal"

labels.required.tenant.rule.value: "The tenancy boundary the request belongs to. Identical vocabulary to the `tenant` extension attribute on the event envelope, including the reserved single-tenant value `local` -- one tenancy token across the bus and the metrics, not two."

labels.required.tenant.forkAnswer.value: "A homelab fork emits tenant=\"local\" on every series and never changes it. This is a defensible value rather than a placeholder: it is already what the event envelope requires of the same fork, and when a second tenant appears it appears as new series alongside, not as a relabelling of the old ones. Queries written `sum by (service)` are unaffected; queries written `sum by (service, tenant)` return one row on a fork and N later without being rewritten."

labels.required.tenant.trustBoundary.value: "This label crosses a trust boundary. In a multi-tenant deployment the value comes from the authenticated principal, never from a request header or a caller-supplied field, and a service configured multi-tenant with no tenancy resolver MUST fail to start rather than emit `local` over everybody's traffic."

labels.required.tenant.busSource.value: "For kind=pubsub and kind=request_reply the authenticated value is the tenant token of the subject the message was DELIVERED on, which NATS account and subject permissions enforce. The envelope `tenant` attribute is set by the publisher -- a caller-supplied field -- and MUST NOT be the label's source."

labels.required.kind.rule.value: "Which surface served the request. The two bus values are the same vocabulary as `pattern` in contracts/events/registry.v1.yaml. It adds no cardinality -- a route belongs to exactly one kind -- and it is what lets an SLO separate an API latency objective from an event-handler one without a regex over route names."

labels.required.kind.streamValue.value: "`stream` is a fourth value and not a flavour of `http` because its duration measures a different quantity: establishment, not completion (see observation.stream). Folding it into `http` would mean one SSE route permanently breaching the service's latency objective, and an SLO cannot separate the two without a regex over route names -- the thing this label exists to avoid. It is present in v1 with no producer because `kind` is closed and compatibility.breaking forbids adding an enum value later; a value that costs nothing unused is cheaper than a metrics.v2.yaml."

labels.required.kind.latencyCoverage.value: "Which routes a latency objective covers is decided by `kind`, selected positively. The platform http latency objective covers kind=http only: every latency SLI, recording rule consumer and alert for it MUST carry the positive matcher kind=\"http\", not kind!=\"stream\", because the negative form also admits kind=pubsub and kind=request_reply, whose handler durations run to the 30s ack deadline. kind=stream durations are establishment times, never pooled with kind=http; a stream route gets its own objective on its own kind=\"stream\" row, named as an establishment objective, or none. The availability SLI keeps its shape: a failed establishment is outcome=\"error\" on kind=stream, and whether a kind=\"stream\" availability row pages is decided by the SLO owner when the first stream route ships, never by widening the http matcher."

labels.required.route.rule.value: "The TEMPLATED identifier of what was served, never the instantiated one. For kind=http: \"<METHOD> <template>\", e.g. \"GET /api/issues/:id\". For kind=pubsub and kind=request_reply: the subject PATTERN from contracts/events/subjects.v1.yaml with its tokens intact, never the subject the message actually arrived on. A request that matches no declared route is recorded as __other__. Falling back to the raw path instead is how an unrouted scanner hitting /a, /b, /c ... turns into unbounded series, and it is the single most common cause of a Prometheus that falls over in month three."

labels.required.route.tailRule.value: "__other__ absorbs the OVER-BUDGET tail as well as the unmatched request. A service with more real routes than maxDistinctValuesPerService allows declares the routes its SLOs and canaries are written against and records every remaining route as __other__. The tail stays measurable in aggregate -- its requests are still in the rate, the error ratio and the histogram -- it just stops being separable by route."

labels.required.route.tailRuleRationale.value: "Without this clause a large API has no conformant move at all. Our own control-plane API exposes on the order of 127 \"<METHOD> <template>\" values; at the declared code ceiling that is 127 x 7 x 16 = 14224 series against a 3000 ceiling, and even at a single code value it is 4064. No value of maxDistinctValuesPerService fixes that, so cardinality.breach (\"the fix is fewer label values\") would have left the contract's own first consumer permanently non-conformant. Collapsing the tail IS fewer label values; this clause says so explicitly rather than leaving each service to infer it."

labels.required.route.tailRuleSelectionI.value: "Which routes stay named is a service-owner decision recorded with the service, not a per-deploy accident: a route that silently moves into the tail takes its SLO history with it and the burn rate resets to no-data. Treat renaming or demoting a declared route as the same class of change as dropping a label value."

labels.required.outcome.rule.value: "Two values, closed, because every error-rate query in the platform is written as a ratio selected on this label. A third value added later would silently change the meaning of every one of them rather than break them."

labels.optional.code.rule.value: "A bounded failure taxonomy, not an HTTP status code. It is deliberately transport-independent so that one alert reads the same on an HTTP handler and on an event consumer. Open for extension within the ceiling: adding a value does not change any `outcome` ratio, so it is additive. Absent on success series. Never present on kind=http as a raw status code."

labels.optional.code.throttledVersusQuot.value: "`throttled` is the service shedding load because it was overloaded -- the service's own failure, and the signal an overload SLO exists to catch. `quota` is the service correctly denying a principal that exceeded a configured limit -- the policy working as designed. Both are outcome=\"error\" so neither is invisible, and both surface as 429."

labels.optional.code.sliExclusionRule.value: "The availability SLI MUST exclude code=\"quota\" from BOTH SIDES of the ratio -- `{outcome=\"error\",code!=\"quota\"}` over `{code!=\"quota\"}`, never over an unselected total. Excluding it from the numerator alone is worse than not excluding it, because the denials stay in the population and are counted as GOOD events. Without the split one noisy tenant burns the service's error budget and, at day 31, blocks every other tenant's releases -- the error budget becomes a denial-of-service vector against the release gate. Written now rather than at day 31 so the gating SLI is written once."

labels.optional.code.sliExclusionBothSid.value: "Quota denials are unbounded in volume, produced by the limit itself, and cheapest to serve exactly when the service is unhealthy -- so they dilute harder than probes do, and probes already needed observation.excluded for the same reason. A service serving 100 req/s with 10 req/s genuinely failing is at 90% availability and must page on the 14.4x tier; one tenant retrying into its quota at 900 req/s moves the measured ratio to 10/1010 = 0.99%, a burn rate of 1.98x, which clears neither paging tier. Numerator-only exclusion stops a noisy tenant from BURNING the budget but lets it HIDE a real outage, which is the worse direction. The latency SLI needs no edit: it selects outcome=\"success\" on both sides, so quota is already out of both."

labels.scrapeAttached.aggregationRule.value: "An SLO, alert or recording rule MUST aggregate away every scrape-attached label, `job` INCLUDED. Prefer the explicit positive form `sum by (service, environment, tenant, kind) (...)`, which cannot silently retain a label a future Prometheus release starts attaching. A query that does not produces a fresh set of series on every rollout, and a burn rate computed over them resets to no-data exactly when a deploy is the thing under suspicion."

labels.scrapeAttached.jobIsNotAnExceptio.value: "`job` is kept in CANARY ANALYSIS QUERIES ONLY, where telling canary from stable is the entire point. In an SLO it is the `pod` failure with a longer fuse: during a rollout the canary pods are scraped under two job values, so one service becomes two SLO rows and the multi-window burn rate over them resets mid-deploy."

labels.scrapeAttached.canarySelection.value: "Canary versus stable is selected on the scrape-attached `job` label, via the Rollout's canary Service and its own ServiceMonitor. The SERVICE MUST NOT emit a version, image tag, commit or pod-template-hash label of its own: those values change on every deploy, so they are unbounded over time in exactly the way the cardinality rules forbid. Build identity lives on platform_build_info."

labels.scrapeAttached.canarySelectionCav.value: "prometheus-operator relabels __meta_kubernetes_service_name to `job`, so `job` is the SERVICE name unless ServiceMonitor.spec.jobLabel names a label on the Service. A canary AnalysisTemplate is therefore given the canary Service name, not the Rollout name, and the two are not the same string."

"The root Service selects canary pods too during a rollout, so with a ServiceMonitor on each the same pod's series exist under two `job` values. It does not breach redFamilySeriesPerReplicaPerTenant -- that ceiling is on EMITTED series -- but it doubles stored series for the rollout's duration, and it is what makes a retained `job` in an SLO a defect rather than a style note."

"After promotion the controller re-points the canary Service selector at the new stable hash, so the same query returns stable traffic. Harmless inside an AnalysisRun, which is scoped to the rollout; a trap for a dashboard or any long-lived rule."

cardinality.rule.value: "Every label value MUST come from a set that is either fixed at build time (a closed or ceilinged enum) or bounded by operator topology (service, environment, tenant). A value derived from request content, from an identity, from a generated id, or from anything that changes on every deploy is forbidden, whatever it is called."

cardinality.ceilings.workedExample.value: "25 routes x (1 success + 6 error codes) x 16 series = 2800, inside the 3000 ceiling."

cardinality.ceilings.workedExampleBasis.value: "The arithmetic is worst case at the DECLARED ceilings, not at the current enum size, because the ceiling is what a conformant service may actually emit. Computed the other way it flattered itself: at 30 routes and the declared code ceiling of 6 the real figure is 3360, over the ceiling, while the file quoted 2250 by multiplying by the four code values that happened to exist. The route ceiling is 25 rather than 30 because the 15s boundary and the `quota` code value together consume the headroom the old figure had, and the fix for a breach is fewer label values."

cardinality.ceilings.maxTenantsRationale.value: "Beyond this a deployment shards by process rather than by label. That is the answer the blast radius asks for before it is the answer cardinality asks for: a single process serving hundreds of tenants is one crash away from being everybody's outage, and per-tenant series are the cheaper half of that problem."

cardinality.breach.value: "A service over its ceiling is non-conformant and the fix is fewer label values, not a higher ceiling. Raising a ceiling is a change to this file with an ADR consequence stated, not a values.yaml override."

cardinality.breachLegalMoves.value: "\"Fewer label values\" is not a demand to delete routes. For the route label the move is labels.required[route].tailRule: declare the routes the SLOs and canaries name and collapse the rest into __other__. A large API reaches conformance by choosing what it measures separately, not by shrinking. Stated because the bare breach rule reads as \"your service is too big to be conformant\", which is not the intent and is not achievable for any real API surface."

exposition.workloadMarkerLabel.rule.value: "A workload carrying this label claims conformance with this file. It is what the scrape-path presence check keys off: the check is \"every workload with the marker has a ServiceMonitor that selects it\", which is decidable from rendered manifests at level 0."

exposition.scrapeIntervalRationale.value: "A canary analysis over a 5m window needs enough samples for rate() to mean something; 30s gives ten. A slower scrape does not fail the contract loudly, it just makes every short-window query noisier than the consumer expects, which is why the ceiling is stated rather than left to each ServiceMonitor."

guarantees.lossIsPermanent.value: "A scrape that does not happen is a sample that never existed. There is no backfill, no replay and no advisory. A service restarting between scrapes loses whatever it counted in between."

guarantees.counterResets.value: "_count and _sum reset to zero on restart. Every consumer expression MUST be built from rate() or increase(), which handle resets. A raw difference of two samples is wrong across any deploy."

guarantees.timestamps.value: "Samples carry scrape time, not event time. Two services' samples for the same second are not simultaneous and must not be compared at sub-scrape resolution."

guarantees.notAnAuditRecord.value: "Never derive billing, audit or compliance evidence from this family. Those are events on PF_AUDIT (ADR-038), which has retention and a delivery guarantee. A metric is a sample."

guarantees.absence.value: "A service that stops exposing produces NO error rate, not a 0% error rate. Every SLO and every canary built on this family must handle absence explicitly -- `absent()` on the SLI, and a canary that must NOT PASS on no-data. A canary that passes because the new version crashed before it served a request is the specific failure this clause exists to prevent."

guarantees.absenceIsNotFailure.value: "Must-not-pass is the requirement; must-fail is not. A homelab fork with no traffic has no data through no fault of the deploy, and a canary that fails closed on it rolls back every release -- the fork-ability contract breaking in the first place a new user meets it. Inconclusive satisfies must-not-pass and pauses for a human. The earlier wording here said \"failure condition on no-data\" and that phrasing is what pushed the worked example into failing closed."

guarantees.emptyIsNotNaN.value: "An empty vector is not NaN. `rate()` over absent series returns nothing, the division never happens, and an `isNaN(result)` guard never fires -- the Argo Rollouts Prometheus provider scores that as an Error against consecutiveErrorLimit, not the Failed the guard intended. Wrap each aggregate in `scalar()`: `scalar()` of an empty vector IS NaN. This is the specific way an absence guard looks correct and does nothing."

members: "adding a required label to an existing family (it changes series identity and silently breaks every rule and dashboard already selecting on the old identity)"
"adding or removing a value of a closed enum (outcome, kind)"
"changing any bucket boundary, including adding one (cross-service histogram_quantile requires identical boundaries, and existing history becomes uncomparable)"
"changing the error classification rule below without changing the metric name -- the quality-gates.md section 3 entry that passes every mechanical check"
"a new `code` value within the ceiling (code is open by design)"
"a new metric family under a new name"
"a new route value within the ceiling"
"a new tenant or environment value (operator data, not contract)"

compatibility.breakingProcedure.value: "A breaking change takes a NEW metric name published alongside the old for at least one minor release, and a metrics.v2.yaml alongside this file. There is no third option; a consumer you cannot see and cannot redeploy is assumed to exist."

errorClassification.principle.value: "outcome=\"error\" iff the service failed to produce the result it promised for a reason inside its own responsibility boundary. A bad request answered correctly is the service working."

errorClassification.http.#1.why.value: "shedding load is a failure to serve, and it is the signal an overload SLO must catch"

errorClassification.http.#2.why.value: "the policy working as designed; visible as an error, excluded from the availability SLI so one noisy tenant cannot burn everybody's budget"

errorClassification.http.#3.why.value: "a validation rejection is correct behaviour; paging on it makes a misbehaving client an outage"

errorClassification.http.#4.why.value: "not the service's failure; its truncated duration is still recorded, and this is stated rather than silently assumed"

errorClassification.bus.precedence.value: "Rows are evaluated top to bottom and the FIRST match wins. The deadline row is first in each table so a handler that overruns and then acks, or overruns and then replies, is a timeout and never a success."

errorClassification.bus.jetstream.rows.#.value: "handler's terminal act came after its effective ack deadline"

"the broker has already scheduled a redelivery, so the late ack did not deliver the promise; the effective deadline is ack_wait from delivery, restarted by each in-progress (+WPI) signal the handler sent"
"handler dead-lettered then terminated a message it rejected as invalid"

"a payload that fails its registered schema or validation is the bus 4xx: the producer's fault, answered correctly; counting it as an error lets a bad producer burn the consumer's budget, the same shape the quota split closes. PF_DLQ depth keeps it visible"
"handler naked, or terminated for any other reason"
"includes the dead-letter on max_deliver exhaustion: that attempt failed like the ones before it"

errorClassification.bus.coreReply.applie.value: "kind=request_reply on an `rq` subject (at-most-once, no ack, no nak, no term)"

errorClassification.bus.coreReply.rows.#.value: "responder passed a deadline it enforces, whether it then replied or abandoned the request"
"on an at-most-once path a reply published after the requester's deadline was never received, so it cannot count as a success"
"responder abandoned the request without publishing a reply, before any deadline"
"the requester sees a timeout, but the cause was the responder's failure, not a deadline"
"replied with a quota denial or overload shedding"
"classified exactly as the two 429 rows under http, so the availability SLI's quota exclusion holds on the bus too"
"replied with a rejection of an invalid request"

errorClassification.bus.invalidRejection.value: "A deliberate dead-letter of an invalid message is outcome=\"success\", not a new `code=\"rejected\"` error excluded from the SLI like quota. The second option spends the last value under the code ceiling and adds a second exclusion every availability SLI has to remember on both sides -- the reserved-value trap observation.excludedRule already rejects. `principle` decides it: a bad request answered correctly is the service working."

errorClassification.bus.noTerminalAct.value: "A handler that crashes before any terminal act records nothing for that attempt: the finally path did not run. The broker redelivers after ack_wait and that attempt is observed. The lost attempt shows as consumer redeliveries, not in this family."

errorClassification.bus.extendedHandlers.value: "A handler that extends with in-progress signals is classified by its terminal act against its effective deadline, and its duration is still delivery to terminal act. It can exceed 30s and land in +Inf. That is the truthful value: an SLO latency threshold is a boundary of at most 30s, so the attempt counts as slow, not missing."

errorClassification.redeliveries.value: "Every path on the bus is at-least-once (ADR-026). A message delivered three times and acked on the third is THREE observations: two errors and one success. The denominator counts delivery attempts, not unique messages, and an error ratio on a retrying consumer is therefore a measure of work done, not of messages lost."

enforcement.statusThisWindow.value: "Binding by review for new first-party control-plane services; advisory for existing ones. The only mechanism running in CI today is the contract's own self-test. Two of the three mechanisms below are specified and not implemented, and this line changes in the same pull request that lands the first of them."

enforcement.mechanisms.contract-self-tes.value: "scripts/metrics-contract_test.ts, run by `task test:scripts` in PR CI"

"An internally inconsistent contract: unsorted or duplicated buckets, le strings that do not match the boundaries, a ceiling whose own worked arithmetic does not fit, a forbidden label that is also required, or a query in the companion document naming a metric or label this file does not declare."

enforcement.mechanisms.scrape-path-prese.value: "A rendered-manifest check over tests/snapshots/: every workload carrying the exposition.workloadMarkerLabel has a ServiceMonitor that selects it, and every first-party control-plane Deployment carries the marker."
"a service that ships with no scrape path at all"

enforcement.mechanisms.exposition-confor.value: "In Kind, scrape the deployed service's /metrics, parse the exposition, and assert the family exists, the bucket boundaries are exactly the pinned ones, the required labels are present, no forbidden label appears, and the series count is under the ceiling."
"a service that ships instrumented to a different shape"

enforcement.mechanisms.sdk-helper.mechan.value: "One helper in the shared SDK (ADR-027) that takes the outcome and the route and does the rest, so the conformant shape is the path of least resistance and the non-conformant one has to be written on purpose."

enforcement.mechanisms.sdk-helper.makesI.value: "nothing by itself; it removes the reason to get it wrong"

adoption.new.definition.value: "a first-party control-plane service whose first deployment merges after 2026-09-27"

adoption.existing.obligation.value: "No retrofit is required in this window and none is scheduled before day 31. An existing service becomes binding the next time it adds or changes request-path instrumentation; until then it is measured against nothing and that is stated rather than pretended otherwise."

adoption.firstConsumer.rule.value: "The canary AnalysisTemplate is written against this file. It is the first consumer, so it is also the first conformance evidence: a template that needs a metric this file does not define means the file is wrong, not the template."

adoption.unaffected.B1-jetstream-metrics.value: "Its metric names come from prometheus-nats-exporter, which is out of scope above. B1 ships the names it already planned to hand over and does not wait for this file."

consumers.sre-alerting-and-slos.role.value: "writes the recording rules, the burn-rate SLOs and the alert rules against this file"
